title: Day 2 — Force Multiplier, Leveraging AI & Email Management

frames.title: Day 2 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 2: Force Multiplier, Leveraging AI and Email Management. We'll start with the executive's exposure and board communication, then move into the force multiplier mindset, cognitive load and systems, and what being a force multiplier means in legal work. After that, we'll look at using AI with precision, and we'll finish with email management.

By the end of today, you'll be ready to manage the executive's exposure, prepare board and investor communications to a higher standard, use AI tools with good judgment, and run the inbox as a control system.

frames.title: Executive Exposure & Board Communication
frames.text: Section 1 of 6: Executive Exposure and Board Communication. We'll cover managing constant executive exposure, board updates, and preparing investor briefings.

frames.title: Managing Constant Executive Exposure
frames.text:
Part of our job is spotting risk hiding inside things that look routine.

A senior executive is exposed all the time: to legal risk, regulation, public opinion, investors and the firm's reputation. Most of that risk doesn't arrive labelled 'dangerous'. It turns up as an ordinary email, a friendly invitation or a contract someone wants signed today. We're often the first to see it, which makes us the first line of defence.

frames.title: Managing Constant Executive Exposure
frames.text:
First, we flag risky emails before they're sent, not after. Next, we check invitations for anything that could look bad. Then, contracts get properly reviewed, never signed on a quick summary. After that, we watch compliance deadlines ourselves. Finally, we handle sensitive messages with discretion by default.

Here's one to think about. Elias is invited to speak on a panel sponsored by a company on the other side of one of the firm's active cases. It arrives as a routine invite. What do you do?

Or a friendly vendor asks for a photo of Elias with their product for their newsletter. It seems harmless. What exposure could it create?

frames.title: Stakeholder & Board Update Communications
frames.text:
A board update isn't just a formal status email. Board members may read it weeks later, or look back at it if something goes wrong, so it needs more precision and a bit more context than an internal note. Same structure as always: what's happening, what it means and what we recommend. We just give enough background to understand it cold.

First, we confirm exactly who'll receive it, because outside directors need something different from the internal team. Next, we lead with what matters for oversight: a decision needed, a risk or a milestone. Finally, it gets a second pair of eyes, however routine it seems.

Think about this. You're drafting a board update on a project that's six weeks behind. How do you give an honest picture without downplaying it or causing panic?

And if a board member emails you directly asking for 'the real story', outside the formal update, how do you respond without a governance mistake?

frames.title: Investor Briefing Preparation
frames.text:
Investors judge both what's in the briefing and how well it was prepared. Every number will be tested, and so will whoever prepared it. Our job is to make sure the executive walks in with the material condensed and checked, not a pile of raw documents.

First, we confirm what the briefing should cover and in what format, because investors often expect a set template. Next, we take every figure from verified, original sources. Finally, we give the executive a heads-up on anything likely to draw a tough question.

Take a second with this one. One figure you were given doesn't match the firm's own recent report. What do you do before the materials go out?

And if an investor asks for 'the pipeline numbers in advance', and Elias hasn't approved sharing anything early, what do you reply?

frames.title: The Force Multiplier Mindset
frames.text: Section 2 of 6: The Force Multiplier Mindset. We'll look at the shift from helper to force multiplier, what that autonomy is and isn't, and how to measure the change.

frames.title: From Helper to Force Multiplier
frames.text:
A helper does what they're told. A force multiplier already has the next answer ready.

The executive asks us to book a room. The helper books the room. The force multiplier books the room, sends the invites, prints the agenda and checks whether the client needs parking. That's not overstepping. It's thinking one step ahead, and having it ready before he asks.

frames.title: From Helper to Force Multiplier
frames.text: First, before a routine task, we ask what he'll probably need next, and prepare that too. Then, we build the habit through steady, reliable work. It grows over time; it doesn't switch on overnight.

frames.title: From Helper to Force Multiplier
frames.text:
After that, we watch for requests that repeat. By the second or third time, we should be anticipating them. Finally, we check ourselves now and then: are we just finishing tasks, or arriving with the next step done?

Here's a situation to work through. For the third week in a row, Elias asks on Monday morning for 'the list of what's due this week.' What would a force multiplier do before next Monday?

frames.title: The Helper Identity vs. the Force Multiplier Identity
frames.text:
The biggest change in this role happens in how we see ourselves, not in our job title.

The helper looks for approval, avoids owning decisions, waits for instructions and measures success by how fast they reply. The force multiplier owns the outcome, sets up the decision, understands how the executive thinks and measures success by how much more he gets done. Same person, same job; a very different way of showing up.

So when a request is unclear, notice your default. Do you ask 'What should I do?', or suggest an approach and ask for a quick OK? And practise attaching a suggestion to every fact you pass on.

Ask yourself: which mindset describes you right now, and which helper habit will you start replacing this week?

frames.title: Why the Force Multiplier Evolution Is Non-Negotiable
frames.text:
In today's executive world, an assistant who only helps becomes a bottleneck. It isn't a personal failing; the job has simply outgrown it.

Executives work fast, in public, with legal exposure and money on the line. If every decision waits for step-by-step instructions, we slow everything down. A force multiplier becomes part of the machinery.

First, we look for signs we're still in helper mode: waiting for instructions on things we've done before, or asking permission for decisions we've already shown we can make. Finally, we change it on purpose: the next familiar request gets a recommendation attached.

Consider this. A colleague prides herself on answering Elias's messages at midnight. She's exhausted, and her daytime work is slipping. What's the better way to add value?

frames.title: Force Multiplier in the Wild
frames.text:
Picture the day before a big pitch. The client suddenly adds requests involving three departments. A helper forwards the emails and hopes. A force multiplier works through it in three steps, always in the same order.

First, we prioritise: what's most time-sensitive, what's waiting on something else, and what the options are. Next, we coordinate: everyone on a shared board or document, with automatic reminders, so nobody's working from an old email. Finally, we close the loop: every task gets an owner, it all comes together in one report, and we confirm the client received it.

Now try this. It's 6 p.m. Finance and marketing have delivered, but legal's conflicts confirmation hasn't arrived, and the pitch is at 9 a.m. What do you do tonight, and what do you tell Elias?

frames.title: What Force Multiplier Autonomy Is — and Isn't
frames.text:
Autonomy is earned and agreed in advance. It's never simply assumed.

Being a force multiplier doesn't mean overstepping, acting like the boss or going off on our own. It means freedom that's been agreed in advance, thinking ahead and carrying things out well. Confidence that knows its limits.

First, before acting on our own on something new, we confirm it's inside the limits we've actually been given. Finally, if we're unsure whether something is ours to decide, that doubt is a signal. Check first.

Take a second with this one. A partner tells you, 'Elias always lets you approve these, just sign off on the $2,000 expense.' Your written limit is $500. What do you say?

frames.title: Measuring the Force Multiplier Transformation
frames.text:
'I cut response time from two days to four hours' lands very differently from 'I'm doing well.'

The good news is this kind of impact can be measured: a smaller inbox, more of his time on important work, fewer last-minute crises and compliance slips, faster replies. Putting a number on even one of those turns a feeling into evidence.

First, we pick one or two measures that fit our role, like reply time, and start noting them, even informally. Finally, when we talk about our performance, we point to real changes.

Picture this. Over a month, your reply time dropped from about 24 hours to 5. How do you present that in your review so it lands, and what else would you put next to it?

frames.title: Cognitive Load & Systems
frames.text: Section 3 of 6: Cognitive Load and Systems. We'll cover reducing the executive's cognitive load, building a system for anything that happens twice, and file naming and version control.

frames.title: Reducing Cognitive Load for Executives
frames.text:
Every open-ended question we send an executive uses up some of his limited decision-making energy. Each 'What would you like to do?' costs him a little, and by midday there's nothing left for the decisions that really matter.

So we do the thinking first: lay out the options, point out the trade-offs and check the risks. Then he only has to choose. A good line sounds like: 'There are three options; B fits best with this quarter's goals.'

frames.title: Reducing Cognitive Load for Executives
frames.text:
Before bringing him any decision, ask yourself what you'd recommend if it were your call, and bring that too.

Here's a situation to work through. A colleague sends Elias: 'Option A: hotel near the court. Option B: hotel near the client. Option C: hotel near the airport. Let me know.' Elias sighs. What's missing, and how would you rewrite it?

frames.title: "If It Happens Twice, It Deserves a System"
frames.text:
The second time you do something by hand is the signal to build a system for it, not the fifth or the tenth.

Helpers solve the same problem over and over. Force multipliers solve it once, then build something so it never needs solving from scratch again. And a system doesn't have to be fancy: a checklist, a template or a simple tracker counts. Think of the weekly report, travel booking, contract approvals or investor updates. Each system has the same parts: the steps, what could be automated, where approval is needed and when to escalate.

Think of one task you've done more than twice this month without a system. What would the first version look like if you built it in fifteen minutes?

frames.title: Operational Excellence & Institutional Accountability
frames.text:
Without clear rules, a high-trust role quietly becomes a high-risk one. The same access that makes us valuable could cause real damage if nobody's keeping track.

So a good assistant knows the rules they work within: what's business and what's personal, how much they can spend, when to escalate and who approves what. And they stay inside those rules on purpose, not by luck, with the limits written down somewhere they can check quickly.

Now picture this. Six months later, finance questions a $3,000 personal expense you approved on Elias's behalf. What written records would protect you, and where should they be?

frames.title: File Naming, Folders & Version Control
frames.text:
In a law firm, the wrong version of a document can get signed, filed or sent to the other side, and file names are the first line of defense.

A good file name tells you what the file is without opening it: the date, the matter, the document type and the version. And every document lives in one place, the firm's document system, not in copies scattered through email and desktops. One source of truth.

frames.title: File Naming, Folders & Version Control
frames.text:
First, one pattern for everything: year, month, day, then matter, document type and version, like 2026-10-02, Harlow, Engagement Letter, v03. Next, we never call a file 'final'. Drafts get version numbers, and the signed or filed copy is marked Executed or As-Filed. Then we save it in the matter's folder, and share a link instead of attaching it. Finally, when edits come back, we save a new version and keep the old ones.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias asks you to send opposing counsel 'the final settlement agreement.' You find four files: 'Settlement final', 'Settlement final 2', 'Settlement v5 EB edits', and a PDF called 'Settlement agreement final clean'. What do you do before sending anything?

frames.title: The Legal EA Force Multiplier
frames.text: Section 4 of 6: The Legal EA Force Multiplier. Here we apply the force multiplier idea to legal work, from authority and boundaries to decision compression and risk buffering.

frames.title: Authority & Boundary Management — EA vs. Legal EA
frames.text:
Knowing what we can decide alone, and what needs approval, keeps a trusted role from becoming a risky one. A legal EA has extra layers on top of normal business rules, and mistakes there can have legal consequences for the firm.

First, as a general EA, we politely refuse approvals we're not authorised for, get written confirmation for budget exceptions, write up verbal approvals afterwards and keep personal and company expenses strictly apart. Finally, as a legal EA, we refuse unauthorised requests for client files, insist on a conflict check before any new matter opens, escalate anything over our financial limit and follow client money rules without exception.

Think about this one. Elias tells you in the corridor, 'Yes, approve the Harlow expert's extra $3,500.' Nothing is in writing. What do you do before the payment goes through?

frames.title: Proactive Risk Mitigation & Strategic Support — EA vs. Legal EA
frames.text:
The best assistants stop problems before they happen, and bring insight, not just information. That's two kinds of high-value work: catching problems early, and strategic support.

First, a general EA catches risks like a problem name on a guest list, a contract about to renew or a typo in a press release. Next, a legal EA tracks compliance filing dates and discovery deadlines, checks signing rules on estate documents and catches unsigned engagement letters before work starts.

Then, for strategic support, a general EA builds a dashboard of key numbers, writes a 30-day action summary after a board meeting and tracks follow-ups. Finally, a legal EA prepares summaries of legal exposure, organises case timelines to show gaps in evidence and builds templates that cut drafting errors.

Picture this. Elias asks for 'a dashboard of the Meridian matter.' You could list every document and date, or build something that shows him what needs attention. Describe the version you'd build.

frames.title: The Legal VA's Force Multiplier Evolution
frames.text:
The move from helper to force multiplier matters even more in legal work, because deadlines, liability and confidentiality raise the stakes.

A traditional legal virtual assistant waits for instructions, finishes assigned tasks and formats documents. A legal force multiplier cuts through the complexity, spots legal risk before it bites, protects the attorney's time and helps decisions happen faster.

First, we notice where our own work sits today: closer to formatting and finishing tasks, or closer to filtering and anticipating risk. Finally, we pick one regular legal task and deliberately move it the force-multiplier way this week.

Here's a situation to think about. A discovery deadline was missed last month because 'nobody flagged it,' even though the notice was in the inbox you manage. What would a legal force multiplier have done differently?

frames.title: Cognitive Relief for Attorneys
frames.text:
An attorney's head is already full. Our job is to take clutter away, not add to it.

They're juggling case strategy, an emotional client, pressure to bring in money, compliance risk and court deadlines. Hand them forty-two unread emails, and we've added to the pile. Say 'three need your legal decision, two are billing approvals, and one is opposing counsel asking for more time', and we've taken a weight off. Same inbox, very different experience.

Try this one. A colleague forwards Elias all 30 emails from a heated client thread 'so he has the full picture.' He asks you what the client actually wants. Write the summary you'd send.

frames.title: Strategic Filtration for Legal Work
frames.text:
Anything that reaches the attorney should have earned their attention. Something can be urgent for admin, legal, money or reputation reasons. Our job is to tell the difference.

First, we flag any risk to the statute of limitations, the legal deadline to file a claim, immediately, every time. Next, we let genuinely non-urgent things wait, like a newsletter draft, even if someone marked it urgent. Then, we escalate press enquiries about active cases straight away; they're a legal and a reputation risk at once. Finally, we sort client requests into those that need the attorney and those a standard reply can handle.

Here's a situation to work through. A client emails in capitals, 'Urgent, urgent, call me now.' It's about parking at the courthouse. Meanwhile, a polite email from opposing counsel mentions 'the response due Friday.' How do you handle both?

frames.title: Operational Architecture for Legal Work
frames.text:
A helper asks what to do next. A force multiplier builds a system so the same crisis never happens again. In a law firm, systems don't just save time; they prevent malpractice. When deadlines live in someone's memory, something eventually slips through.

First, we build a dashboard for litigation deadlines. Next, we write down a standard process for taking on a new client, so it doesn't depend on one person remembering the steps. Finally, we add a checklist for reconciling client trust money, consistent file names and a tracker for discovery responses.

Then consider this. The team says fixing deadline tracking 'needs a new software purchase.' What could you build this week with a shared spreadsheet to solve most of the problem?

frames.title: Decision Compression
frames.text:
Attorneys are paid for their judgment, so our job is to get them to the decision fast.

Compare two emails. One says, 'Here's the 60-page contract.' The other says, 'Three clauses differ from our standard: indemnification is wider, payment terms are down to ten days and the arbitration venue has moved to Texas. Please review sections 4, 7 and 11.' The second lets the attorney spend their time on the decision, not hunting for it. That's decision compression.

frames.title: Decision Compression
frames.text:
Before sending anything long for review, ask yourself the three most important things the reviewer needs to know, and lead with those.

Take a second with this one. A colleague forwards Elias a 90-page expert report with the note 'FYI.' Elias asks, 'What do I need from this?' What should the note have said?

frames.title: Risk Buffering for Legal Work
frames.text:
Protecting the attorney from avoidable mistakes is one of the most trusted things we do, and every risk we catch builds credibility.

The habits are simple. We track compliance deadlines in every jurisdiction, check signatures and witnesses as a standard step, protect privileged information, write down approvals and watch trust account procedures. And no engagement letter means no billable work, even for a client who's been with us for years.

Now picture this. It's 4:50 p.m., a will signing is about to happen, but only one witness is present and the state requires two. Everyone wants to 'just get it done.' What do you do?

frames.title: Leveraging AI with Precision
frames.text: Section 5 of 6: Leveraging AI with Precision. We'll start with the rules for AI use in the legal industry, then what a large language model is, and how to pick the right tool for each job.

frames.title: Before You Begin: AI Use in the Legal Industry
frames.text:
Before we talk about what AI can do, let's agree the standard it always has to meet. Three rules.

First, the firm's and the attorney's preferences come first; some are happy with AI, some aren't, and some only allow it for certain tasks. Second, anything involving legal judgment stays with a human. AI can help draft, but the attorney makes the call. And third, confidentiality. Pasting privileged client information into the wrong tool isn't a small slip; it can be a real legal problem.

So before using AI on any task, check what this firm and this attorney allow on this matter, and check whether what you're pasting is privileged.

frames.title: Before You Begin: AI Use in the Legal Industry
frames.text:
If you're not sure it's appropriate, ask first, rather than asking forgiveness later. These rules are a filter every AI technique must pass, not a disclaimer we read once.

Here's one to think about. Elias asks you to 'run the Meridian deposition transcript through AI and pull out the contradictions.' Before you do anything, what do you need to check, and what do you say to him?

And what if another partner on a shared matter has said, 'No AI on my matters, ever'?

frames.title: The Digital Edge
frames.text:
Three digital skills together take repetitive work off our plate: using AI properly, simple automation and clear charts.

Using AI properly means real work from start to finish, like a full first draft, or turning a 50-page report into a five-point morning brief, not just playing with clever prompts. Automation means little rules so things happen by themselves, like a task appearing when a certain client emails. And a basic chart in Excel or Tableau shows a budget far more clearly than a table of numbers.

frames.title: The Digital Edge
frames.text:
First, we pick one repeating task and automate it, even with just an email rule. Next, we learn a basic charting tool. Then, we use the three skills together, not just one. Finally, once a month, we look for the next thing to automate.

Take a second with this one. Every Friday, someone asks, 'Where are we on the billing numbers?', and you spend an hour pulling them together. What digital fix would stop that fire from starting each week?

frames.title: What Is a Large Language Model?
frames.text:
An AI chatbot predicts the next likely word. It doesn't look anything up, so sounding confident tells us nothing about whether it's right.

That's the most important thing to understand about tools like ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. They learned patterns from huge amounts of text, and produce the words most likely to come next. That's why they write so fluently. It's also why they sometimes invent a fact, a date or a legal case, with exactly the same confidence as something true.

So we check every specific fact, date or figure ourselves, especially anything going to a client, a court or the executive.

frames.title: What Is a Large Language Model?
frames.text:
Made-up answers tend to appear where the tool doesn't really know, filling the gap smoothly instead of admitting it. So 'how would I check this?' becomes an automatic question for every output we use.

Here's a situation to work through. An AI draft of a client letter confidently says a filing deadline is 'within 21 days.' The actual rule for this court is 14. What does that tell you, and what's your checking habit from now on?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. True or false: an LLM looks up facts in a database before answering. Take a second.

The answer is false. It generates a statistically likely response. Anything true in that response is true because the pattern happened to match reality, not because it was looked up.

frames.title: Core AI Terms an EA/PA Needs
frames.text:
A few AI terms come up all the time, and knowing them helps us avoid the most common mistakes.

A prompt is our instruction; a better prompt gets a better answer. A hallucination is when the tool states something false with complete confidence. The context window is its working memory; paste in too much and it gets fuzzy towards the end. And tokens are the chunks of text it counts, roughly three-quarters of a word each, which is why long documents can hit a limit.

frames.title: Core AI Terms an EA/PA Needs
frames.text: In practice, keep what you paste to a sensible length, and remember token limits are real on longer documents, even on premium accounts.

frames.title: Core AI Terms an EA/PA Needs
frames.text:
Treat every output as something to check, not something to trust.

Now a situation to think about. A colleague pastes a client's full name, medical details and settlement amount into a free AI account to 'tidy up the wording.' What's the risk, and what should she have done?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. You paste a 40-page contract and ask for a summary of section 12. The AI's answer mixes up details from section 3. What most likely happened? Is it A, context window strain, where it lost precision across a long document? B, section 12 was too complex for the AI to understand? C, the contract format wasn't supported? Or D, the AI refused the request? Take a second.

The answer is A, context window strain. When a document is long, precision degrades across it, so paste just the relevant section when precision matters.

frames.title: Your AI Toolkit — Three Modes, Different Jobs
frames.text:
AI can do three quite different jobs, and choosing the right one avoids the costliest mistakes.

The first is creating new text, like a polite decline, a bio or a summary of a messy thread. The second is pulling out exact information without changing it, like every date or action item in a long email chain. And the third is connecting a trigger to an action, like filing attachments automatically or alerting us when a VIP emails.

frames.title: Your AI Toolkit — Three Modes, Different Jobs
frames.text: First, before opening a tool, decide which of the three jobs the task needs. Then, for exact facts, use extraction, because a generative tool might subtly change a detail.

frames.title: Your AI Toolkit — Three Modes, Different Jobs
frames.text:
After that, to connect a trigger to an action, use an automation tool, not a chatbot. Finally, if you're unsure and exact facts or figures are involved, choose extraction. A changed detail is the costlier mistake.

Try sorting three tasks: pull every deadline out of a 20-email thread, draft a thank-you note to a client, and get an alert whenever opposing counsel emails. Which mode fits each?

frames.title: Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini — Practical Differences
frames.text:
The three big AI tools have different strengths, but the same risks. All three can invent facts, all three have memory limits, and all three may learn from what we paste, depending on the account.

Beyond that, they suit different jobs. Claude tends to handle long documents well and lets us control the tone. ChatGPT has the widest range of add-ons and is quick for trying drafts. Gemini lives inside Gmail, Docs and Calendar, so it works with live information, which means our security habits matter even more.

frames.title: Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini — Practical Differences
frames.text: Whichever tool you use, the same checks apply. And when you're automating inside Google Workspace, start simple, like Gmail filters, before reaching for anything advanced.

frames.title: Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini — Practical Differences
frames.text:
Then pick the tool for the job. For quick drafting and trying versions, ChatGPT is often the practical choice. For anything working on live email, documents or calendars, Gemini fits, with stricter security habits.

Here's a situation to think about. A colleague built a complex script that automatically files client emails into Drive folders. She's leaving, and nobody else understands it. What simpler automation could replace it, and why is simpler better here?

frames.title: Email Management
frames.text: Section 6 of 6: Email Management. We'll treat email as a control system, then look at inbox triage, the daily routine and the priority matrix.

frames.title: Email Is a Control System, Not Cleanup
frames.text:
Before we act on any email for the executive, we need to know exactly what we're allowed to do.

There are three levels of access. With full access, we can read, reply, file and send in his name. With draft and review, we prepare replies, and he approves them before they go. With triage only, we sort and flag, and he replies himself. Using a higher level than we've been given isn't helpful. It's crossing a line.

frames.title: Email Is a Control System, Not Cleanup
frames.text: First, confirm your level, and don't assume it's the same as your last job. Then, on draft and review, wait for his OK, even if you're sure it's right.

frames.title: Email Is a Control System, Not Cleanup
frames.text:
After that, on triage only, resist drafting replies he didn't ask for. Finally, if your level isn't clear, ask rather than guess.

Think about this. You're on draft and review. A client emails at 6 p.m. asking to confirm tomorrow's 9 a.m. meeting, and Elias is on a flight. What can you do now, and what has to wait for him?

frames.title: What High-Performing Inbox Triage Looks Like
frames.text:
Top assistants handle eighty to ninety percent of routine emails themselves, without sending them up the line.

That can sound scary, but think about a typical inbox: confirmations, scheduling, simple questions, updates. Most of it doesn't need the executive personally. The first step is honest: find out how much we handle ourselves today. Then we close the gap one kind of email at a time.

frames.title: What High-Performing Inbox Triage Looks Like
frames.text: First, spot the routine emails you're still escalating out of habit. Those are the quickest wins. Then build the judgment to handle them, checking your calls against what he'd actually have wanted.

frames.title: What High-Performing Inbox Triage Looks Like
frames.text:
After that, as you handle more, guard the two big risks: never miss a critical deadline, and never breach confidentiality. Finally, keep the inbox at or near zero every day, as visible proof the system's working.

Here's a situation to work through. It's going well, and then you notice an email with a filing deadline buried in a thread you archived as routine. What changes in your triage from now on?

frames.title: The Daily Routine
frames.text:
A simple routine at the start, middle and end of the day means nothing important slips through the cracks, and the executive starts every day informed instead of surprised.

First, the morning scan: 15 to 30 minutes to spot anything urgent, clear the junk and prepare a short briefing. Next, the midday review: draft replies, chase anything waiting and confirm the afternoon's meetings. Finally, the end-of-day review: nothing urgent left hanging, and tomorrow set up.

Now build it around Elias. He's in court by 9 a.m. three days a week and checks messages at 12:30 during the lunch break. When do your check-ins happen on those days, and what's ready for him at each one?

frames.title: The Morning Briefing, In Practice
frames.text:
The morning briefing replaces the inbox; if it's as long as the inbox, it isn't working. Picture Elias with his first coffee. He doesn't want 30 emails. He wants to know what needs him today, in a minute. The inbox, digested.

First, read the whole inbox yourself, but never just forward it. Next, boil each item down to one line: what it is and where it stands. Then, put the most urgent first, like an approval that expires today.

frames.title: The Morning Briefing, In Practice
frames.text:
After that, keep it to a handful of lines. Finally, send it at the same time every morning.

Here's one to work through. Elias says he stopped reading your briefings because they're 'as long as my inbox.' Rewrite yesterday's briefing in three parts: needs you, handled and heads-up.

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. What best distinguishes high-performing email management from average? Is it A, forwarding every email so nothing is missed? B, deleting anything that looks unimportant? C, replying to everything within 5 minutes? Or D, handling 80 to 90 percent of operational emails independently, with zero missed deadlines? Take a second.

It's D. It's about independent, reliable handling of the bulk of email, not speed or forwarding volume.

frames.title: The Priority Matrix
frames.text:
Deciding how urgent something is comes first, because that decides how fast you respond.

Everything falls into one of two top groups. The first can't wait: legal deadlines, major clients, the press, money approvals and genuine crises. Those go to the executive right away. The second is important, but not worth interrupting him for: new business, partnerships, board matters and vendor deals. For those, we have a drafted response ready within a few hours.

frames.title: The Priority Matrix
frames.text: First, decide the tier before you do anything else. Next, Tier 1 goes to the executive straight away, no exceptions. Then, Tier 2 gets a response within two to four hours.

frames.title: The Priority Matrix
frames.text:
After that, if you can't tell the tier, treat it as Tier 1 until you know. Over-escalating costs less than missing something. Finally, look back at your calls now and then, and learn from the wrong ones.

Speed round. Call the tier for each: a court clerk's notice. A partnership inquiry. The bar association newsletter. A reporter asking for comment. A vendor saying an invoice is 60 days overdue.

And one more. The monthly email from the cleaning company normally goes in Tier 3. This month it says they found an unlocked filing cabinet full of client files after hours. What tier is it now, and what do you do?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. A media inquiry with a deadline tomorrow just landed. Under the Priority Matrix, is it A, something to batch with the newsletter? B, not worth flagging? C, Tier 1, notify the executive immediately? Or D, Tier 2, draft a response in two to four hours? Take a second.

It's C. Media inquiries with a hard deadline sit squarely in Tier 1: immediate escalation.

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Now it's your turn. In the Force Multiplier Challenge, you'll anticipate what a vague executive request really needs, write a prompt that actually runs and produces real output, handle a messy combined scenario, then clear a real inbox, building your own filing system and catching a hidden phishing attempt.
